screens.title: Data Privacy in Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn concrete, practical methods that Fabric provides to keep sensitive transaction data private while preserving ledger integrity. We focus on Private Data Collections, the configuration file that controls them, how chaincode stores and retrieves private data, and the lifecycle controls that enforce retention. Then we introduce Zero-Knowledge Proofs as an advanced option to prove statements without revealing the underlying secret. Private Data Collections let a subset of organizations share confidential content while the channel still records a hash so all parties can verify integrity. This reduces the need for separate channels and simplifies operations. Zero-Knowledge Proofs are typically produced off-chain and verified on-chain, enabling selective disclosure like proving eligibility without exposing raw values. You will see a supply-chain scenario where a manufacturer shares pricing with a supplier, code and command examples to deploy a private collection, and common pitfalls such as reading private data from a non-member peer. By the end you will know when to choose a PDC, how to configure blockToLive for retention, and what role ZKPs can play in high-privacy workflows.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › Data Privacy Overview
Data Privacy in Fabric
Private Data Collections and Zero-Knowledge Proofs for selective disclosure

Fabric separates confidentiality from integrity: private data lives only on authorized peers while a digest is recorded on the channel ledger so all members can confirm a transaction happened without seeing the secret. This makes PDCs an operationally lighter alternative to creating separate channels for every private relationship.

In this lesson
PDC design and lifecycle
Define collections, use PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData, and manage retention with blockToLive.
Coming up
ZKP integration
How proofs are generated off-chain and verified on-chain to preserve extreme privacy.
Explore Key Topics
Private Data Collections
Subset sharing with only a hash on the public ledger.
collections_config.json
Defines members, retention and dissemination parameters.
Zero-Knowledge Proofs
Prove statements without revealing the underlying secret.
Private vs Public
Data flows and proofs
A compact visual: private values travel peer-to-peer between authorized members and are stored in the private database. The network ledger receives only the hash, which proves integrity without revealing content. ZKPs add an option to verify a condition about private data without exposing it at all.
Why this matters
Enterprises need to balance confidentiality with auditability. PDCs and ZKPs provide patterns that preserve privacy while keeping a verifiable channel-wide record.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your attention on practical skills and design judgments. First, you will be able to distinguish Private Data Collections from separate channels and explain the trade-offs in management and operational overhead. Second, you'll design and implement a collections_config. json file to control who stores private data, how many peers receive it, and how long it lives. Third, you will understand the private-data lifecycle: how data is passed transiently to chaincode, stored only on member peers, referenced publicly by a hash, and purged based on blockToLive. Fourth, you'll grasp the fundamentals of Zero-Knowledge Proofs and how to integrate them with Fabric chaincode for selective disclosure, including the common technique of generating proofs off-chain and verifying them on-chain. For each skill we'll show a concrete example and the common pitfalls, such as trying to read private data from a non-member peer or setting blockToLive too low for availability. Achieving these means you not only configure privacy, but reason about retention, auditing, and advanced cryptographic patterns for high-assurance workflows.

screens.title: What is a Private Data Collection (PDC)?
screens.narratorSegment: A Private Data Collection is a named grouping that allows a subset of organizations on a channel to exchange confidential state without exposing that content to all channel members. The key claim is simple: keep the secret off the shared ledger while committing only a hash to the public record so others can verify the transaction's integrity. Concretely, private values are stored in the private database of authorized peers such as CouchDB or LevelDB. The public ledger holds a hash that binds the private data to the transaction history, preserving immutability without disclosure. For example, in a supply chain the manufacturer and a supplier can keep pricing private while retailers still see the proof that a price update occurred. A common misconception is that private data is stored on every peer or that the hash reveals the content; neither is true. Only collection members store the data, and a hash cannot be reversed to reveal the underlying value. Takeaway: PDCs let you preserve confidentiality and auditability together. Reflect: which confidential fields in your own systems should be private values and which can remain on the public ledger?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: PDCs store sensitive values only on authorized peers while committing a hash to the public ledger for integrity.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is a PDC?
Private Data Collection
A confidential store limited to collection members
Private data is kept in each member peer's private database; only the hash is recorded on the channel ledger. This preserves immutability while preventing disclosure of sensitive content to non-members.
Analogy
Think of a PDC as a sealed envelope passed only among certain participants, while the channel ledger records a receipt proving an envelope was exchanged.
Example
Manufacturer shares price list with specific supplier; retailers only see a hash proving the update occurred.
Key Takeaway
PDCs give confidentiality plus verifiable integrity via hashes on the ledger.
How it works
1) Client includes private payload in transient fields sent with proposal.
2) Endorsing peers that are collection members receive and store the private data in their private DB and compute read/write set hashes.
3) The ordering service receives the transaction and the public ledger records only the hash while private contents are disseminated off-ledger to collection peers.
Common mistake
Expecting private data to be readable from peers not listed in the collection policy. Non-members only see the hash and cannot retrieve the secret.

screens.title: Where private data lives and what the ledger stores
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the split between private databases and the public ledger is central to correct PDC design. Private values are stored only on authorized peers in their respective private state databases, commonly CouchDB or LevelDB. The public ledger records a hash of the private read/write set for each transaction, which provides an immutable anchor that any member can use to verify that the private content existed and was consistent with the transaction. Practically, that means a peer not in the collection will never receive the private value; it will only observe the hash and the normal public state changes. A concrete scenario: Org1 and Org2 share confidential appraisal values in a collection. Their peers store the details locally and replicate to required peers based on requiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount. Org3 sees only the hash in the block. A common misconception is believing the hash allows reconstruction of the secret; cryptographic hashes are one-way, so the only way to see the data is membership in the collection or having obtained it externally. Key takeaway: the ledger keeps integrity, private DBs keep confidentiality—both are required for auditable privacy.

keyIdea.title: Storage split
keyIdea.text: Private DBs hold confidential content; the public ledger holds a one-way hash for integrity and auditability.

content.html:
Process Flow › Private DB vs Ledger
Private database
Stores actual private values only for collection members. Options include CouchDB or LevelDB on each authorized peer.
Dissemination
Private data is disseminated only to peers that belong to the collection and up to maxPeerCount entries for resilience.
Local privacy
If a peer is not part of the collection, it won't receive private content and reads will return nil or an error.
Public ledger
Records only a hash of the private read/write set. This hash proves the transaction and allows non-members to verify integrity without access to secrets.
Immutability
The hash in the block is immutable and stays even if private data is later purged from member peers.
Audit pattern
Auditors can compare stored private data to the hash for verification, or use ZKPs to validate properties without seeing raw data.
Key Takeaway

PDCs separate confidentiality from integrity: private DBs hold secrets, the ledger holds their one-way proof.

screens.title: collections_config.json — fields explained
screens.narratorSegment: The collections_config. json file declares the properties of a private data collection and is central to how Fabric enforces confidentiality. Each collection entry must include a name and a policy: the policy defines which organizations are collection members and uses familiar MSP-based expressions such as OR and AND. RequiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount determine how many peers must receive the private data and how many may receive it for replication and resilience. blockToLive controls retention: a zero means keep private data indefinitely; a positive integer causes Fabric to purge private data after that many blocks. memberOnlyRead decides whether non-members are allowed to read private data if they somehow obtain it; it defaults to true for stricter confidentiality. A concrete example is a collection that names Org1 and Org2 in the policy, sets requiredPeerCount to 1, maxPeerCount to 2, and blockToLive to zero for indefinite retention. Common pitfalls include mis-typed MSP names in the policy or selecting a blockToLive so low that legitimate peers that were offline miss the data. Key practice: validate your collection JSON against intended membership and retention requirements before chaincode definition.

keyIdea.title: Config essentials
keyIdea.text: collections_config.json determines who stores private data, how widely it is disseminated, and how long it is retained.

content.html:
Definition › collections_config.json
Primary fields
Each collection entry controls membership, dissemination, and retention.
name
Unique collection identifier used by chaincode.
policy
Endorsement policy that lists org MSPs allowed to be members, using OR/AND constructs.
requiredPeerCount / maxPeerCount
Controls minimum and maximum peer recipients for private data to balance resilience and exposure.
blockToLive
Number of blocks after which private data is purged from the private DB; zero means keep forever.
memberOnlyRead
When true, only members may read the private data even if others obtain the hash.
Practical notes
Validate MSP names and policy logic, align requiredPeerCount with your availability plan, and choose blockToLive with auditability in mind.
Scenario
Short-lived bids benefit from a non-zero blockToLive so bids are purged after the auction closes and compliance is enforced automatically.
Pitfall
Setting blockToLive too low can prevent late-joining or temporarily offline peers from ever receiving necessary private state.

screens.title: Using PutPrivateData / GetPrivateData and transient fields
screens.narratorSegment: Chaincode interacts with private collections via a small set of APIs. The most common are PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData. PutPrivateData stores a value in the named collection under a key and impacts only the private database of collection peers. GetPrivateData retrieves that value from the calling peer's private DB. The correct flow for secret inputs is to pass them in the transient field of the proposal so they are not recorded in the proposal payload that could leak through logs. For example, an asset transfer can pass an appraisal value in transient data, have endorsing collection peers store it with PutPrivateData, and commit a transaction whose public ledger entry contains only the hash. A common misconception is embedding private values in normal transaction arguments; that leaks them into the public proposal and can expose secrets. When you write chaincode, always accept private fields from transient data and call PutPrivateData for storage. Also build error handling for GetPrivateData returning nil so your client can detect permission or membership issues. Practically, this pattern preserves confidentiality while enabling verification by hash. Using PutPrivateData / GetPrivateData and transient fields means use transient fields for private inputs; use putprivatedata to store and getprivatedata to retrieve private entries from collection member peers.. In practical terms, chaincode calls and passing private inputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Chaincode APIs
keyIdea.text: Use transient fields for private inputs; use PutPrivateData to store and GetPrivateData to retrieve private entries from collection member peers.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › PutPrivateData / GetPrivateData
Pattern
Accept private inputs via transient, then call PutPrivateData to persist them to the collection members' private DB.
// Pseudo-code for a chaincode function
func CreateAsset(stub ChaincodeStubInterface) error {
  transientMap, _ := stub.GetTransient()
  props := transientMap['asset_properties'] // confidential
  // store in the collection
  err := stub.PutPrivateData('Org1MSPPrivateCollection', props['assetID'], []byte(props))
  // compute and return
}
Practical guidance
Always send private data in transient; never as plain chaincode args. Handle nil returns from GetPrivateData and surface clear errors to clients so they can distinguish permission problems from absent keys.
Example
The sample asset-transfer-private-data chaincode expects appraisedValue in transient and stores it in the collection; clients must pass the transient map when invoking.
Misconception
Do not place private fields in the visible argument list of a proposal; that can leak sensitive data in logs or to observers.

screens.title: PDCs vs Separate Channels
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric offers multiple ways to isolate data: Private Data Collections and separate channels. The key difference is scope and operational cost. Separate channels create an entirely separate ledger and ordering sequence, isolating transactions completely but increasing network complexity and operational overhead for every new private relationship. Private Data Collections keep a single channel for shared interactions while providing fine-grained confidentiality between subsets of organizations. This simplifies governance and reduces the number of ledgers to manage. A concrete example: If two organizations inside a larger consortium frequently exchange private pricing, a PDC avoids creating a whole new channel for those two. A common misconception is that PDCs are less secure; in fact they provide equivalent confidentiality when configured correctly because private data is never placed on the public ledger and only authorized peers store it. However, channels can still be appropriate when transaction ordering or total isolation is required. Key takeaway: prefer PDCs for many pairwise or small-group confidentiality needs and reserve channels for strict isolation or completely separate administrative domains. PDCs vs Separate Channels means pdcs reduce overhead and maintain a single channel while channels provide full isolation; choose based on governance and operational cost.. In practical terms, choosing the right privacy mechanism. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choosing privacy
keyIdea.text: PDCs reduce overhead and maintain a single channel while channels provide full isolation; choose based on governance and operational cost.

content.html:
Comparison › PDCs vs Channels
Private Data Collections
  • Confidential data shared among collection members only.
  • Hash recorded on the common channel ledger for integrity.
  • Lower operational overhead than managing additional channels.
Good when you need selective confidentiality within a shared governance domain.
Separate Channels
  • Complete ledger separation and isolated ordering.
  • Higher administrative and operational cost for each channel.
  • Appropriate when administrative boundaries differ or ordering must be isolated.
Choose channels when full isolation and separate governance are required.
Key Takeaway
PDCs are the operationally lighter option for selective confidentiality; channels provide hard separation at greater complexity.

screens.title: Private Data Lifecycle and blockToLive
screens.narratorSegment: Private data in Fabric follows a lifecycle you must plan for. First, a client sends sensitive values in transient fields with a proposal. Endorsing peers that are collection members receive the transient data, compute the read/write set, store the private content in their private DB, and produce the corresponding hashes. The transaction goes to ordering and the public ledger records only the hash. Over time, blockToLive controls whether private data remains: when the configured number of blocks has passed, Fabric purges the private entries from member peers' private databases while the hash remains on the ledger forever. A practical scenario is a bidding process where you set blockToLive to purge bids after award finalization to meet compliance. A common mistake is setting blockToLive too low, causing late-joining or temporarily offline peers to miss private data. Another is assuming purged private data can be reconstructed from the hash; hashes are one-way and cannot recreate the original. Key takeaway: choose blockToLive intentionally based on availability, auditability, and regulatory retention requirements. Private Data Lifecycle and blockToLive means private data is accepted via transient, stored by member peers, hashed on the ledger, and purged per blocktolive settings.. In practical terms, from transient input to purge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Private data is accepted via transient, stored by member peers, hashed on the ledger, and purged per blockToLive settings.

content.html:
Process Flow › Private Data Lifecycle
1
Transient input
2
Endorse & store
3
Order & hash
4
Purge (blockToLive)
Example
A sealed bid process sets blockToLive so bids are purged after finalization; only the hash remains to show that bids existed at the time.
Pitfall
A very low blockToLive means offline peers may never see private state, causing inconsistent local histories across members.
Key Takeaway
blockToLive is a retention control: pick a value that balances privacy, compliance, and the need for peers to access historical private state.

screens.title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs — the concept
screens.narratorSegment: Zero-Knowledge Proofs allow one party to convince another that a statement is true without revealing any additional information. The classic formulation contains three properties: completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge. In practice for Fabric, the prover generates a compact proof off-chain and submits that proof as part of a transaction. Chaincode then verifies this proof using a verification library. A concrete example: a user proves they are over 18 without revealing their exact birthdate, or a participant proves sufficient funds without disclosing actual balances. Applying ZKPs inside Fabric usually means generating proofs in a client application and having on-chain verification ensure the proof is valid before performing sensitive actions. A common misconception is that ZKPs eliminate all need for private storage; they do not replace PDCs but can complement them by enabling proofs about private data while minimizing disclosure. Key takeaway: ZKPs extend privacy by letting participants prove properties about secrets, and Fabric's chaincode model supports integrating verification libraries for this purpose. In practical terms, prove truth without revealing facts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: ZKPs let you prove a statement about secret data without revealing the secret; generate proofs off-chain and verify them on-chain in Fabric.

content.html:
Definition › Zero-Knowledge Proofs
Zero-Knowledge Proofs in a nutshell
Prover demonstrates a truth about secret data without revealing the secret itself. Fabric can accept a proof byte array as part of a transaction and validate it in chaincode.
Completeness
A valid proof convinces the verifier.
Soundness
A false statement cannot be proven except with negligible probability.
Zero-knowledge
No extra information beyond the truth of the statement is revealed.
Example
Prove account balance exceeds a threshold without revealing exact balance: client constructs proof off-chain and chaincode verifies it before allowing a transfer.

screens.title: Integrating ZKPs with Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating Zero-Knowledge Proofs into Fabric applications typically follows a two-part architecture. First, the prover generates the proof off-chain using a ZKP library suited for the chosen curve or construction. This off-chain step can operate in a trusted client environment where the secret data is available. Second, the proof is submitted as part of a transaction proposal and chaincode runs a verification function using an appropriate verification library. If the proof verifies, the chaincode proceeds with state changes; if not, it rejects the proposal. This separation leverages Fabric's endorsement and ordering flow: endorsements can include the verification outcome, and ordering preserves the on-chain evidence as part of the transaction. A practical example is an eligibility check where the client proves membership in a group without revealing identity; the chaincode accepts the proof and records the approved action while continuing to keep identifying data private. Misconceptions include thinking verification is free; cryptographic verification can be computationally expensive and may require careful performance planning. Key takeaway: Fabric's chaincode model supports ZKP verification, but you must design for off-chain proof generation, on-chain verification, and performance trade-offs.

content.html:
Architecture › ZKP integration
Off-chain: proof generation
Client constructs proof from private data using a ZKP toolkit. Proofs are compact byte arrays submitted with the transaction.
Why off-chain?
To avoid exposing secrets and to use optimized native libraries for proof construction.
On-chain: verification
Chaincode uses a verification library to check the proof; verification success gates state changes. Keep in mind verification costs and endorsement policies.
Performance note
Verification can be CPU-intensive; design endorsement and chaincode execution with that cost in mind.
Example flow
Client generates a proof that a user meets a condition, submits it with the proposal, chaincode verifies the proof and, on success, executes a private-state update or records a public proof marker.

screens.title: When to use PDCs and common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding to use a Private Data Collection requires weighing confidentiality, availability, audit, and operational simplicity. Use PDCs when you need selective confidentiality among a subset of organizations that otherwise participate in the same channel. Favor PDCs when operational overhead of channels is prohibitive. Common pitfalls include forgetting to include the collections_config. json at chaincode definition time, mismatching MSP names or policy logic so intended members are excluded, and setting blockToLive too low, which can cause late-joining peers to permanently miss private data. Another mistake is placing private inputs in regular arguments instead of the transient map, which risks leaking secrets. Mitigations: validate your collections file, test queries from both member and non-member peers during deployment, set dissemination counts consistent with your resilience needs, and document retention requirements with legal and operational teams before choosing blockToLive. For audit scenarios, consider combining PDCs with ZKPs to allow auditors to verify properties without accessing raw private data. Final thought: design privacy as a policy and operational workflow, not just a technical flag. When to use PDCs and common pitfalls means plan collections as part of governance: validate config, align retention with compliance, and test access patterns to avoid surprises.. Design Guidance › When to use PDCs
Decision criteria
  • Need selective confidentiality among channel members without creating many channels?
  • Desire a single shared governance model and ledger for broader interactions?
  • Do retention requirements allow purging private data after a predictable period?
Common pitfall
Missing or misconfigured collections_config.json at chaincode definition time causes expected privacy protections to fail.
Mitigation
Run staged deployments and queries as both member and non-member, and document retention rules with stakeholders.

Treat PDC configuration as part of your governance process; test membership, dissemination, and retention before production roll-out.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn concrete, practical methods that Fabric provides to keep sensitive transaction data private while preserving ledger integrity. We focus on Private Data Collections, the configuration file that controls them, how chaincode stores and retrieves private data, and the lifecycle controls that enforce retention. Then we introduce Zero-Knowledge Proofs as an advanced option to prove statements without revealing the underlying secret. Private Data Collections let a subset of organizations share confidential content while the channel still records a hash so all parties can verify integrity. This reduces the need for separate channels and simplifies operations. Zero-Knowledge Proofs are typically produced off-chain and verified on-chain, enabling selective disclosure like proving eligibility without exposing raw values. You will see a supply-chain scenario where a manufacturer shares pricing with a supplier, code and command examples to deploy a private collection, and common pitfalls such as reading private data from a non-member peer. By the end you will know when to choose a PDC, how to configure blockToLive for retention, and what role ZKPs can play in high-privacy workflows.

These objectives focus your attention on practical skills and design judgments. First, you will be able to distinguish Private Data Collections from separate channels and explain the trade-offs in management and operational overhead. Second, you'll design and implement a collections_config. json file to control who stores private data, how many peers receive it, and how long it lives. Third, you will understand the private-data lifecycle: how data is passed transiently to chaincode, stored only on member peers, referenced publicly by a hash, and purged based on blockToLive. Fourth, you'll grasp the fundamentals of Zero-Knowledge Proofs and how to integrate them with Fabric chaincode for selective disclosure, including the common technique of generating proofs off-chain and verifying them on-chain. For each skill we'll show a concrete example and the common pitfalls, such as trying to read private data from a non-member peer or setting blockToLive too low for availability. Achieving these means you not only configure privacy, but reason about retention, auditing, and advanced cryptographic patterns for high-assurance workflows.

These applied objectives move from configuration to operation. First, you will manage private data lifecycle by selecting appropriate blockToLive values and understanding the trade-offs between retention and availability. Second, you will handle dissemination counts so requiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount match your resilience and confidentiality needs. Third, you'll detect and recover from common mistakes such as missing collections_config. json or reading private data from a peer that isn't a collection member, which often surfaces as empty responses or permission errors. Fourth, you'll reason about audit patterns, including how hashes on the public ledger preserve integrity even when private data is purged, and how ZKPs can allow auditors to validate properties without seeing raw data. Each objective is practical: you will edit the collections JSON, pass private inputs in transient fields, deploy the chaincode with the collections config, and observe data lifecycle behavior. By practicing these steps you reduce operational errors and ensure privacy meets compliance requirements.

A Private Data Collection is a named grouping that allows a subset of organizations on a channel to exchange confidential state without exposing that content to all channel members. The key claim is simple: keep the secret off the shared ledger while committing only a hash to the public record so others can verify the transaction's integrity. Concretely, private values are stored in the private database of authorized peers such as CouchDB or LevelDB. The public ledger holds a hash that binds the private data to the transaction history, preserving immutability without disclosure. For example, in a supply chain the manufacturer and a supplier can keep pricing private while retailers still see the proof that a price update occurred. A common misconception is that private data is stored on every peer or that the hash reveals the content; neither is true. Only collection members store the data, and a hash cannot be reversed to reveal the underlying value. Takeaway: PDCs let you preserve confidentiality and auditability together. Reflect: which confidential fields in your own systems should be private values and which can remain on the public ledger?

Understanding the split between private databases and the public ledger is central to correct PDC design. Private values are stored only on authorized peers in their respective private state databases, commonly CouchDB or LevelDB. The public ledger records a hash of the private read/write set for each transaction, which provides an immutable anchor that any member can use to verify that the private content existed and was consistent with the transaction. Practically, that means a peer not in the collection will never receive the private value; it will only observe the hash and the normal public state changes. A concrete scenario: Org1 and Org2 share confidential appraisal values in a collection. Their peers store the details locally and replicate to required peers based on requiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount. Org3 sees only the hash in the block. A common misconception is believing the hash allows reconstruction of the secret; cryptographic hashes are one-way, so the only way to see the data is membership in the collection or having obtained it externally. Key takeaway: the ledger keeps integrity, private DBs keep confidentiality—both are required for auditable privacy.

The collections_config. json file declares the properties of a private data collection and is central to how Fabric enforces confidentiality. Each collection entry must include a name and a policy: the policy defines which organizations are collection members and uses familiar MSP-based expressions such as OR and AND. RequiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount determine how many peers must receive the private data and how many may receive it for replication and resilience. blockToLive controls retention: a zero means keep private data indefinitely; a positive integer causes Fabric to purge private data after that many blocks. memberOnlyRead decides whether non-members are allowed to read private data if they somehow obtain it; it defaults to true for stricter confidentiality. A concrete example is a collection that names Org1 and Org2 in the policy, sets requiredPeerCount to 1, maxPeerCount to 2, and blockToLive to zero for indefinite retention. Common pitfalls include mis-typed MSP names in the policy or selecting a blockToLive so low that legitimate peers that were offline miss the data. Key practice: validate your collection JSON against intended membership and retention requirements before chaincode definition.

Chaincode interacts with private collections via a small set of APIs. The most common are PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData. PutPrivateData stores a value in the named collection under a key and impacts only the private database of collection peers. GetPrivateData retrieves that value from the calling peer's private DB. The correct flow for secret inputs is to pass them in the transient field of the proposal so they are not recorded in the proposal payload that could leak through logs. For example, an asset transfer can pass an appraisal value in transient data, have endorsing collection peers store it with PutPrivateData, and commit a transaction whose public ledger entry contains only the hash. A common misconception is embedding private values in normal transaction arguments; that leaks them into the public proposal and can expose secrets. When you write chaincode, always accept private fields from transient data and call PutPrivateData for storage. Also build error handling for GetPrivateData returning nil so your client can detect permission or membership issues. Practically, this pattern preserves confidentiality while enabling verification by hash. Using PutPrivateData / GetPrivateData and transient fields means use transient fields for private inputs; use putprivatedata to store and getprivatedata to retrieve private entries from collection member peers.. In practical terms, chaincode calls and passing private inputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Fabric offers multiple ways to isolate data: Private Data Collections and separate channels. The key difference is scope and operational cost. Separate channels create an entirely separate ledger and ordering sequence, isolating transactions completely but increasing network complexity and operational overhead for every new private relationship. Private Data Collections keep a single channel for shared interactions while providing fine-grained confidentiality between subsets of organizations. This simplifies governance and reduces the number of ledgers to manage. A concrete example: If two organizations inside a larger consortium frequently exchange private pricing, a PDC avoids creating a whole new channel for those two. A common misconception is that PDCs are less secure; in fact they provide equivalent confidentiality when configured correctly because private data is never placed on the public ledger and only authorized peers store it. However, channels can still be appropriate when transaction ordering or total isolation is required. Key takeaway: prefer PDCs for many pairwise or small-group confidentiality needs and reserve channels for strict isolation or completely separate administrative domains. PDCs vs Separate Channels means pdcs reduce overhead and maintain a single channel while channels provide full isolation; choose based on governance and operational cost.. In practical terms, choosing the right privacy mechanism. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Private data in Fabric follows a lifecycle you must plan for. First, a client sends sensitive values in transient fields with a proposal. Endorsing peers that are collection members receive the transient data, compute the read/write set, store the private content in their private DB, and produce the corresponding hashes. The transaction goes to ordering and the public ledger records only the hash. Over time, blockToLive controls whether private data remains: when the configured number of blocks has passed, Fabric purges the private entries from member peers' private databases while the hash remains on the ledger forever. A practical scenario is a bidding process where you set blockToLive to purge bids after award finalization to meet compliance. A common mistake is setting blockToLive too low, causing late-joining or temporarily offline peers to miss private data. Another is assuming purged private data can be reconstructed from the hash; hashes are one-way and cannot recreate the original. Key takeaway: choose blockToLive intentionally based on availability, auditability, and regulatory retention requirements. Zero-Knowledge Proofs allow one party to convince another that a statement is true without revealing any additional information. The classic formulation contains three properties: completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge. In practice for Fabric, the prover generates a compact proof off-chain and submits that proof as part of a transaction. Chaincode then verifies this proof using a verification library. A concrete example: a user proves they are over 18 without revealing their exact birthdate, or a participant proves sufficient funds without disclosing actual balances. Applying ZKPs inside Fabric usually means generating proofs in a client application and having on-chain verification ensure the proof is valid before performing sensitive actions. A common misconception is that ZKPs eliminate all need for private storage; they do not replace PDCs but can complement them by enabling proofs about private data while minimizing disclosure. Key takeaway: ZKPs extend privacy by letting participants prove properties about secrets, and Fabric's chaincode model supports integrating verification libraries for this purpose. Integrating Zero-Knowledge Proofs into Fabric applications typically follows a two-part architecture. First, the prover generates the proof off-chain using a ZKP library suited for the chosen curve or construction. This off-chain step can operate in a trusted client environment where the secret data is available. Second, the proof is submitted as part of a transaction proposal and chaincode runs a verification function using an appropriate verification library. If the proof verifies, the chaincode proceeds with state changes; if not, it rejects the proposal. This separation leverages Fabric's endorsement and ordering flow: endorsements can include the verification outcome, and ordering preserves the on-chain evidence as part of the transaction. A practical example is an eligibility check where the client proves membership in a group without revealing identity; the chaincode accepts the proof and records the approved action while continuing to keep identifying data private. Misconceptions include thinking verification is free; cryptographic verification can be computationally expensive and may require careful performance planning. Key takeaway: Fabric's chaincode model supports ZKP verification, but you must design for off-chain proof generation, on-chain verification, and performance trade-offs.

Deciding to use a Private Data Collection requires weighing confidentiality, availability, audit, and operational simplicity. Use PDCs when you need selective confidentiality among a subset of organizations that otherwise participate in the same channel. Favor PDCs when operational overhead of channels is prohibitive. Common pitfalls include forgetting to include the collections_config. json at chaincode definition time, mismatching MSP names or policy logic so intended members are excluded, and setting blockToLive too low, which can cause late-joining peers to permanently miss private data. Another mistake is placing private inputs in regular arguments instead of the transient map, which risks leaking secrets. Mitigations: validate your collections file, test queries from both member and non-member peers during deployment, set dissemination counts consistent with your resilience needs, and document retention requirements with legal and operational teams before choosing blockToLive. For audit scenarios, consider combining PDCs with ZKPs to allow auditors to verify properties without accessing raw private data. Final thought: design privacy as a policy and operational workflow, not just a technical flag. Let's summarize the core ideas to carry forward. First, Private Data Collections let a subset of organizations share private content while recording only a hash on the channel ledger, providing confidentiality plus verifiable integrity. Second, collections_config. json governs membership, dissemination counts, and retention via blockToLive, and must be included at chaincode definition time to take effect. Third, chaincode APIs PutPrivateData and GetPrivateData are used together with transient fields for private inputs; avoid putting secrets in plain arguments. Finally, Zero-Knowledge Proofs can complement PDCs by allowing statements about private data to be verified on-chain without revealing the underlying secrets. Keep these points in mind as design constraints and tools when implementing privacy-sensitive Fabric applications. To close, keep three compact rules in mind. One: configure collections_config. json correctly—membership, dissemination, and blockToLive are the levers of privacy and retention. Two: always pass private inputs in transient fields and use PutPrivateData/GetPrivateData so secrets never appear on the public proposal or ledger. Three: use Zero-Knowledge Proofs when you need to prove facts about private data without revealing the data itself; generate proofs off-chain and verify them in chaincode. These three practices together let you build systems that are confidential, auditable, and flexible for enterprise needs.
